summary: Rosario Strait light on Burrows Island near Anacortes, first lit 1 April 1906; Coast Guard keepers to 1972; station owned by the Northwest Schooner Society, restoration under way.

lens.note: A modern optic replaced the Fresnel lens in the lantern room in the early 1990s (LighthouseFriends).

structures.note: 34-foot square tower attached to the fog-signal building (LighthouseFriends); wood on a stone foundation (USLHS).
Duplex keepers' quarters (USLHS). Boarded up after automation (LighthouseFriends).
Built north of the duplex in 1952 for the officer in charge; torn down (LighthouseFriends).

access.note: Grounds open; dwelling and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The USLHS record says the station is not open to the public.

facts.ownership: nonprofit (owner and manager of the light station); most of the island is Burrows Island State Park

events.note: Board asked Congress for $15,000 for a light and fog signal on the southwest point (LighthouseFriends).
Congress appropriated the money on 24 February 1903 after repeated requests (LighthouseFriends).
Site obtained by condemnation on 28 June 1904 for $350 (LighthouseFriends).
Lit 1 April 1906, white light with a red sector from a fourth-order Fresnel lens (LighthouseFriends; USLHS gives the year).
Daboll trumpet in the fog-signal building (LighthouseFriends).
On 25 June 1914 assistant keeper Michael Ludescher towed a disabled launch with seven persons to the station (Bulletin 1914).
Fixed white until 1 May 1927, then a group of two flashes every fifteen seconds (LighthouseFriends).

Storm of 21-24 October, which swept Washington and Oregon, described in the Bulletin's issue of 1 November 1934 (the same issue carries the Tillamook Rock report of the 21 October storm). Burrows Island is listed among the stations where considerable damage was done.

March 1936: keeper John O'Rourke kept a boat party in sight after a second landing, then took them in and fed and dried them. Seven months later he sheltered two boys lost in a rowboat in fog and took them to the mainland the next morning. Names withheld.
Station staff reduced from three men to two (LighthouseFriends).
Automated when the remaining Coast Guard personnel left (LighthouseFriends).
Forty acres conveyed to Washington State Parks; the state has since acquired most of the island as Burrows Island State Park (LighthouseFriends).
Station offered to an eligible nonprofit under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act of 2000; five nonprofits applied (LighthouseFriends).
Secretary of the Interior signed paperwork on 23 June 2010 to begin transfer to the Northwest Schooner Society; title to pass after lead cleanup (LighthouseFriends).
Coast Guard contractors removed contaminated soil and replaced the failing roof on the keeper's dwelling (LighthouseFriends).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Every source read gives 1906 (USLHS record, LighthouseFriends). No conflict found.
The USLHS record says the station is not open to the public; LighthouseFriends says the grounds are open and the dwelling and tower are closed. The story gives both: grounds open, buildings closed.

The USLHS record and LighthouseFriends name the Northwest Schooner Society as owner of the light station; LighthouseFriends also says title is to pass only after the Coast Guard's lead clean-up. The story says the Society is restoring the station and does not state a completed transfer. Most of the 486-acre island is Burrows Island State Park.

LighthouseFriends gives a 34-foot tower; the USLHS record gives 27 feet from base to the centre of the lantern and 57 feet above mean high water for the light. These are different measures. The story gives the record's base-to-lantern figure beside LighthouseFriends' tower height.

The Bulletin passage on the 21-24 October storm is in the issue of 1 November 1934, not the February 1934 issue. The year is therefore 1934. An earlier version of this record gave 1933, inferred from the wrong issue; that is corrected.

notes_for_editor: Sources: USLHS place record with keeper roster (58 lines; NARA keeper registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory); LighthouseFriends (facts only, short quotations, plus the Anacortes American of 5 April 1906 as LighthouseFriends prints it); Lighthouse Board reports 1899, 1900, 1901 (scan pages; the 1901 estimates page, scan page 66 = printed page 46, was viewed as an image and the $15,000 Burrows line in the Thirteenth District list is confirmed; the 1899 and 1900 passages are OCR'd, so the evidence quotes avoid the garbled 'fog-signal' word); Lighthouse Service Bulletins 1914 (PDF page 31) and 1934 (issue of 1 November 1934, PDF page 25, storm damage). Not read: the NRHP nomination (the NPGallery PDF for 100010694 returned an image, not text); the 2024 NRHP listing in the record is unverified. The 1906 newspaper: a Chronicling America search returned no readable page; the Anacortes American's words are as LighthouseFriends prints them. The 1903 appropriation and 1904 site purchase come from LighthouseFriends only; the Act and the Board's 1903-04 reports were not found. The storm: the Bulletin's passage gives 'October 21 to 24' in the issue of 1 November 1934; the year follows from that issue, and the same issue reports the 21 October storm at Tillamook Rock. Height: the USLHS record gives 57 ft (17.4 m) above mean high water and 27 ft (8.2 m) from base to lantern centre; LighthouseFriends gives a 34-foot tower. The story gives the record's 27 ft beside LighthouseFriends' 34 ft as different measures. Wikipedia's figure is not used. Range 7.0 nm in the record is not verified and not used. Living people: the 1936 boat party and the two boys are not named; roster names after about 1960 are copied from the USLHS roster as printed (Richard P. Johnson, Floyd Shelton and others) and only the 1969-1972 officer in charge (David J. Grotting) is named in the story, in his public role. The roster gives no gender for Lulu Pfaff or Ann Thomas, and the story does not describe them as women. The Northwest Schooner Society is named as owner in the USLHS record and LighthouseFriends; the story says it is restoring the station and does not claim a completed title transfer.
